01: Your manager says "just add some AI to it". You need to know whether the thing you are about to build learns from data at all, or is a pile of if-statements wearing a trenchcoat.
02: You have a spreadsheet. Sometimes there is an answer column, sometimes there is not. What you are allowed to do next depends entirely on that.
03: Your fraud model was trained in January. It is now November and fraudsters have changed tactics. Retraining from scratch every night costs 40 GPU-hours.
04: Two systems both predict house prices. One keeps all 50,000 training houses in memory forever; the other keeps two numbers. Only one of them fits on a phone.
05: Your model scored 0.94 in the notebook and 0.61 in production. Nothing about the code changed.
06: Before you spend three weeks building something, you want to know whether this problem has ever been solved by ML, and what it looked like when it worked.
07: You have been handed a vague business request and a database login. There are eleven things to do and doing them in the wrong order wastes a month.
08: A library throws: expected shape (32, 28, 28, 1), got (32, 784). You need to know what those numbers mean before you can fix anything.
09: "Reduce customer churn" is not a thing a model can predict. You need to turn an English sentence into a target column, a loss function and a success metric.
10: The data you need is split across a CSV someone emailed you, a Postgres table, a REST API with rate limits, and a web page with no API at all.
11: You have 60 columns you have never seen. Before modelling anything you need to know which ones are broken, skewed, constant, or secretly a copy of the target.
12: Two people run the same algorithm on the same dataset. One gets 0.71, the other 0.89. The difference is entirely what they did to the columns first.
13: Your dataset has age in years (18–70) and income in rupees (20,000–2,000,000). Gradient descent now cares about income roughly ten thousand times more than age, for no good reason.
14: You are feeding pixel values (0–255) into a neural network that expects small inputs, and your weights are exploding on the first epoch.
15: The column says "Bangalore", "Delhi", "Mumbai". Your model does arithmetic. It cannot multiply a weight by the word Mumbai.
16: Your pipeline has 12 numeric columns needing scaling, 4 categorical ones needing one-hot, and 2 that should be left alone. Doing this by hand breaks the moment a column moves.
17: You scaled the training data, fitted a model, then forgot to scale the test data the same way. Your score is garbage and the bug is invisible.
18: Your target is right-skewed income. A linear model assumes roughly symmetric errors, so it is systematically wrong at both ends.
19: Taking a log fixed the skew on one column and made another column worse, because that column has zeros and negatives.
20: Age behaves nothing like a straight line against your target: risk is high for teenagers, low in middle age, high again later. A single slope cannot say that.
21: One column contains C2, C3, C4 and also 1, 2, 3. It is two variables that got stuffed into one cell.
22: Your model sees the timestamp 2026-10-05 14:32:00 as a meaningless number, when the useful signal is "Monday" and "afternoon".
23: 300 rows out of 10,000 have a missing value. Someone suggests deleting them. Whether that is fine or catastrophic depends on why they are missing.
24: A column is 12% missing and you cannot drop the rows. Fill with the mean and you shrink the variance; fill with the median and you ignore the distribution's shape.
25: The missing values are in a categorical column. There is no mean of "Bangalore".
26: Height is missing for a row, but weight and age are present, and those three move together. Filling with the global mean throws that relationship away.
27: Five columns are each 10% missing, in different rows. You want a fill that respects how all five columns relate to each other at once.
28: One customer has a logged income of 9,000,000. Your mean, your standard deviation, your scaler and your regression slope are all now reporting on that one person.
29: Your column is clearly skewed, so the mean and standard deviation are themselves distorted by the outliers you are trying to find.
30: You know the top and bottom 1% are data-entry noise, but you cannot afford to delete the rows.
31: You have length, width and height as three columns, and the model never figures out on its own that what matters is volume.
32: You added more and more features expecting better accuracy. Past about 40 features it got worse, and training slowed to a crawl.
33: You have 200 correlated features and need 2 axes you can plot, without just deleting 198 columns at random.
34: You have five months of ad spend and revenue. Someone asks what revenue to expect if you spend ₹10,000 more next month.
35: Two models predict house prices. One is off by ₹2 lakh on average, the other explains 82% of the variance. Those are different claims and your boss wants one number.
36: Price depends on area AND bedrooms AND age AND distance to the metro, all at once, and they interact with each other.
37: The closed-form solution needs to invert a p×p matrix. You have 50,000 features, so that matrix has 2.5 billion entries and does not fit in RAM.
38: You have 10 million rows. Computing the gradient over all of them for every single parameter update means one update per coffee break.
39: The scatter plot is a clear curve. A straight line is going to be wrong in the middle and wrong at both ends, forever, no matter how much data you add.
40: Your degree-12 polynomial fits the training points perfectly and is wildly wrong between them. Your straight line is mediocre everywhere. You need a vocabulary for that difference.
41: Your model has 80 features, several highly correlated, and the fitted coefficients are enormous and flip sign if you resample the data.
42: You have 500 features and believe maybe 20 matter. You want the model to tell you which 20 and set the rest to exactly zero.
43: You have 500 correlated features and want sparsity, but Lasso keeps arbitrarily picking one of each correlated pair and dropping the others.
44: You need a line that separates two classes, and you want to understand the simplest possible rule for nudging that line when it gets a point wrong.
45: A linear model happily outputs −3.2 and 7.8. You asked it for a probability, which has to live between 0 and 1.
46: Squared error on a classification problem gives you a non-convex loss with bad gradients. You need a loss that comes from what the model is actually claiming.
47: Your cancer screening model is 99% accurate. Only 1% of patients have cancer. The model predicts "no cancer" every single time.
48: Your fraud detector flags 500 transactions. Catching more fraud means flagging more innocent customers. You need to be able to state that trade-off numerically.
49: You now have 7 classes instead of 2, and "precision" is suddenly 7 different numbers that need to become one.
50: Logistic regression gives you one probability. You have 10 handwritten digits and need 10 probabilities that sum to 1.
51: The two classes are separated by a circle, not a line. Your logistic regression draws a line and gets 60%.
52: Your logistic regression overfits with 400 features, and the solver throws a convergence warning you have been ignoring.
53: The model outputs 0.43. Is that fraud? Your choice of cutoff silently decides your precision and recall, and nobody wrote it down.
54: You need a model that a loan officer with no maths background can read off a printout and explain to a rejected customer.
55: The tree has 14 features to choose from at the root. It needs a number that says which split actually made the groups purer.
56: The target is a continuous price, not a class. There is no entropy of a price.
57: Your tree grew to depth 28, has one leaf per training row, and scores 100% on train and 61% on test.
58: You have four mediocre models at 72–75% accuracy and no time to build a better one. They make different mistakes.
59: Three classifiers disagree on a row. Two say yes, one says no, but the one that says no is 99% confident and the other two are at 51%.
60: Your decision trees have high variance: resample the data and you get a completely different tree. You want to average that noise away.
61: Bagged trees are still correlated, because every tree keeps picking the same one dominant feature at the root.
62: You are bootstrapping anyway, so roughly a third of the rows were never shown to each tree. Setting aside a separate validation set wastes data you already have.
63: The model works and the stakeholder asks which features drive it. The built-in importance numbers inflate high-cardinality columns.
64: Your single train/test split says 0.86. You re-split with a different random seed and get 0.79. Which number do you report?
65: Averaging independent trees fixes variance but not bias. You want each new model to specifically attack what the previous one got wrong.
66: You now have two ensemble strategies that both improve accuracy, and you need to know which one to reach for when the problem is underfitting versus overfitting.
67: AdaBoost reweights rows, which only works cleanly for classification. You want the same "fix the previous model's mistakes" idea for a continuous target.
68: Gradient boosting works but takes 40 minutes on your dataset, overfits without careful tuning, and chokes on missing values.
69: XGBoost takes an hour on 10 million rows, and your dataset is mostly high-cardinality categorical columns you had to one-hot into 3,000 features.
70: Your five models each have different strengths. Averaging them equally wastes that information: you want to learn how much to trust each one.
71: You have no time to train anything. Someone wants a prediction for one new customer right now, and you have 10,000 labelled past customers.
72: Infinitely many lines separate your two classes perfectly on the training data. They will not perform equally on new data.
73: Your classes overlap slightly, so no straight line separates them perfectly, and the hard-margin SVM simply has no solution.
74: The classes are separable, but only by a curve. Mapping to a higher-dimensional space would fix it, except that space has 10,000 dimensions and you cannot afford to build it.
75: You have 20,000 spam emails and 50,000 vocabulary words. Modelling how all those words co-occur needs more data than exists.
76: You have 100,000 customers, no labels at all, and marketing wants four segments by Friday.
77: You do not know how many clusters there are, and K-Means makes you commit to a number before you start.
78: Your data has one dense blob, one crescent shape and thirty scattered noise points. K-Means forces every one of those noise points into a cluster.
79: PCA squashed your 50-dimensional clusters into an unreadable blob, because the structure you care about is curved, not linear.
80: Your dataset is 99.2% legitimate transactions. Every model you train learns to predict "legitimate" and stops there.
81: Your grid search has 6 hyperparameters and would need 15,625 model fits. You have time for about 60.
82: The notebook scores 0.89. Now it needs to answer HTTP requests at 3am, with the exact same preprocessing, and tell you when the world has drifted away from its training data.
